entities.name: 2006 Horn of Africa food crisis
entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary: In 2006, an acute shortage of food affected the countries in the Horn of Africa, as well as northeastern Kenya. The United Nations's Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) estimated on January 6, 2006, that more than 11 million people in these countries may be affected by an impending widespread famine, largely attributed to a severe drought, and exacerbated by military conflicts in the region. Warnings from the FAO and international agencies highlighted the vulnerability of pastoral and agro-pastoral communities whose livelihoods depended on livestock and seasonal crops. Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, and Djibouti faced the most severe impacts, with pastoralist populations in the arid lowlands particularly devastated. The crisis prompted emergency food aid distributions and humanitarian interventions, yet underlying structural vulnerabilities—conflict, weak governance, and climate variability—persisted. The 2006 crisis underscored how environmental shocks and political instability compound to create humanitarian emergencies in the Horn of Africa, a pattern that would recur in subsequent droughts and famines throughout the 2010s.
